rationale: Cover-uncover test distinguishes tropia from phoria — a high-yield EOM examination concept tested at MBBS level.
Painful pupil-involved CN III palsy with posterior communicating artery aneurysm is a classic red-flag — distinguishing it from medical (diabetic) CN III palsy is a critical clinical decision.
Comitant vs incomitant distinction is the most clinically important classification in strabismus — incomitant implies a neurological cause requiring urgent workup.
In CN VI (abducens) palsy the affected eye cannot abduct — this incomitant esotropia worsens on ipsilateral gaze, a pattern students frequently confuse with medial rectus overaction.
Distinguishing refractive-origin headache (asthenopia) from headache caused by raised ICP is a core referral decision in community ophthalmology.
WHO xerophthalmia classification stage X1B (conjunctival xerosis with Bitot's spots) is frequently confused with X1A in MCQs — students must know the staging sequence.
Vitamin A supplementation dosing and timing for children 12–59 months is a frequently tested NPCB/NRHM fact — students commonly confuse the dose for different age groups.
The sympathetic ophthalmia prevention rule (enucleation within 14 days of penetrating injury) is a classic high-yield OP fact — students frequently get confused about which procedure prevents it.
Exenteration for mucormycosis (rhinocerebral mucormycosis with orbital extension) is a key emergency indication — the threshold decision is life-threatening spread vs tissue preservation.
Alkali > acid severity in chemical burns, and the critical rule that irrigation must begin IMMEDIATELY before any other assessment, is a classic OP exam trap.
The 'do not patch — Fox shield' rule for open globe injuries is a key management distinction students must internalise for clinical practice.

WHO ICD-11 blindness threshold (visual acuity worse than 3/60 or visual field <10 degrees) is frequently tested alongside India-specific NPCBVI definitions — distinguishing the two is a common exam trap.
NPCBVI target: cataract is the leading cause of avoidable blindness in India and the focus of the national programme — students must know the leading cause framing for community medicine exams.
